title: How many children could be playing Fire in the Mountain?
description: In a game of Fire in the Mountain no one gets out on two calls but some children get out on a third. The board finds the lowest common multiple of the first two numbers, keeps the options that are its multiples, and then uses the third call to drop any option that ten divides.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number that two numbers divide exactly is a multiple of their lowest common multiple, and a number that a third number does not divide exactly leaves something over. Watch for children who pick ninety because it is a multiple of eighteen and forget the call of ten.

source: Children are playing Fire in the Mountain. No one got out when 6 was called out or when 9 was called out, but some got out when 10 was called out. How many children could have been playing initially?
video_script.why: The child can find a lowest common multiple of two numbers and test multiples against a third clue.
video_script.substitution: A number of children that six and nine both divide exactly is a multiple of eighteen, and a call of ten that sends some children out means ten does not divide it.
video_script.anchor: children standing in groups, with the six options for the number of children listed beside them
video_script.payoff_line: The children could be seventy two or thirty six
maths_rules: 6 = 2 x 3 and 9 = 3 x 3; most 2s is one, most 3s is two, so LCM = 2 x 3 x 3 = 18
the number of children is a multiple of 18
72 = 4 x 18, 36 = 2 x 18, 90 = 5 x 18, so these stay
45 = 2 x 18 + 9 and 3 is less than 18, so these go
ten does not divide the number, since some children got out on 10
90 = 9 x 10, so no one would get out on 10, and 90 goes
72 = 7 x 10 + 2 and 36 = 3 x 10 + 6, so some children are left over on 10 and both stay
check: 72 = 12 x 6 = 8 x 9 and 36 = 6 x 6 = 4 x 9, with none left over on 6 and on 9
video_script.design: The game is read as in the worklist: a call makes groups of that size and a child left over is out. The lowest common multiple of the first two calls is found and the options are filtered, as in the book's solved example.
open_questions: The book does not describe how Fire in the Mountain is played; the rule that a call makes groups of that size and a child left over is out is taken from the worklist steps.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about a game called Fire in the Mountain.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>When six was called out, no one got out. The same happened when nine was called out.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>But when ten was called out, some children got out.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>How many children could have been playing at the start?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: children split into groups of one size; a left-over child glows and is marked out; a call card says six divides the number exactly

marks.m1: the children split into groups of the called size
marks.m2: a left-over child glows and is marked out
marks.m3: the call cards 6 and 9 each say divides the number exactly

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>When a number is called, the children make groups of that size.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A child left over is out. If every child fits in a group, no one is out.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That means six divides the number of children exactly, and so does nine.

beats.on_screen: Given: called 6, no one out; called 9, no one out; called 10, some out. Options: (a) 72 (b) 90 (c) 45 (d) 3 (e) 36 (f) None of these

marks.m1: the three calls and the options are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, when six and nine were called, no one got out. When ten was called, some children got out.

beats.on_screen: To find: how many children could have been playing

marks.m1: the words how many children could have been playing are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find how many children could have been playing.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: LCM of 6 and 9. 6 = 2 x 3 and 9 = 3 x 3. Most 2s: one. Most 3s: two. LCM = 2 x 3 x 3 = 18

marks.m1: the heading LCM of 6 and 9 is written
marks.m3: the most 2s and the most 3s are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the lowest common multiple of six and nine, because both divide the number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six is two times three, and nine is three times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Take the most twos, which is one, and the most threes, which is two.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Two times three times three gives eighteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: keep the multiples of 18. 72 = 4 x 18, 36 = 2 x 18, 90 = 5 x 18. 45 = 2 x 18 + 9 and 3 is less than 18: both go.

marks.m1: 72 = 4 x 18 and 36 = 2 x 18 are written with ticks
marks.m2: 90 = 5 x 18 is written with a tick
marks.m3: 45 = 2 x 18 + 9 and the 3 are written and crossed out

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, keep the options that are multiples of eighteen. Seventy two is four times eighteen, and thirty six is two times eighteen.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ninety is five times eighteen, so it stays too.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Forty five is two times eighteen plus nine, and three is smaller than eighteen. Both go.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: use the call of 10. Some got out, so 10 does not divide the number. 90 = 9 x 10: goes. 72 = 7 x 10 + 2 and 36 = 3 x 10 + 6: stay.

marks.m1: the call of 10 and the words 10 does not divide the number are written
marks.m2: 90 = 9 x 10 is written and crossed out
marks.m3: 72 = 7 x 10 + 2 is written with a tick
marks.m4: 36 = 3 x 10 + 6 is written with a tick

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, use the call of ten. Some children got out, so ten does not divide the number exactly.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ninety is nine times ten, so no one would get out. Ninety goes.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Seventy two is seven times ten plus two.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Thirty six is three times ten plus six. Both leave children over, so both stay.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check. 72 = 12 x 6 = 8 x 9 and 36 = 6 x 6 = 4 x 9, with none left over. On 10: 2 left over and 6 left over.

marks.m1: 72 = 12 x 6 = 8 x 9 is written with groups drawn
marks.m2: 36 = 6 x 6 = 4 x 9 is written with groups drawn
marks.m3: the left-over children on a call of 10 glow: 2 and 6

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Check by putting each number back in the game. Seventy two makes twelve groups of six and eight groups of nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Thirty six makes six groups of six and four groups of nine, with none left over.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Groups of ten leave two children over, or six, so some children get out.
